overview: This file traces Japanese railway development and related U.S. diplomatic reporting from 1930 to 1939. Its earlier documents cover the Nagasaki rail extension serving Shanghai steamships, plans for the Kanmon undersea tunnel, annual Japanese railway reports, railway corruption trials, the unsuccessful Japan–Soviet Manchurian freight conference, and political conflict over the presidency of the South Manchuria Railway. The final and most detailed group concerns a proposed Japanese purchase of 42 used Lehigh Valley Railroad locomotives, including repair costs, financing terms, equipment specifications, possible shipment from Jersey City, and the State Department’s discreet effort to discourage a four-year credit transaction without issuing a formal prohibition.

subfiles.title: Report on completion of the Nagasaki wharf railway extension
subfiles.from: Henry B. Hitchcock, U.S. consul at Nagasaki
subfiles.about: Reports the opening of a railway extension connecting Nagasaki’s central station with the Dejima wharf used by express steamships.
subfiles.summary: The extension allowed passengers arriving from Shanghai to transfer directly from steamship to trains for central and eastern Japan. Hitchcock places it within a larger transportation program that included the planned Kanmon tunnel and the Ariake railway line, which was intended to shorten the Nagasaki–Moji route. He predicted that improved rail-water connections and future freight facilities would revive Nagasaki as a gateway to China, southern Asia, the Philippines, the East Indies, and Australasia.

subfiles.title: Neville despatch transmitting the 1928–1929 railway annual report
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, chargé d’affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: Transmits two copies of the Japanese Department of Railways annual report for the year ending March 31, 1929.
subfiles.summary: Neville forwards the annual report under separate cover from the embassy in Tokyo. The report itself is not included in the OCR text.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Forbes despatch on railway scandals
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes (referenced despatch)
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to despatch no. 107 concerning the Tokyo District Court judgment in the Echigo Railway and Yamate Express Tramway scandal.
subfiles.summary: The filing note cross-references the relevant political report in decimal file 894.00 P R/37. It identifies Forbes’s January 13, 1931 despatch as the source for the railway-corruption judgment.

subfiles.title: Report excerpt on the Echigo and Yamate railway scandals
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes
subfiles.about: Summarizes convictions and appeals arising from corruption involving the Echigo Railway and Yamate Express Tramway.
subfiles.summary: The Tokyo District Court imposed suspended prison terms and fines on former education minister Kazuta Kobashi and former railway vice minister Sango Satake, while railway and tramway officers received fines for bribery. Kobashi argued that money received from the Echigo Railway was merely a token of thanks for political assistance. All defendants initiated appeals.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Dooman report on the Manchurian freight conference
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman (referenced report)
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to a report on the January 1931 freight conference between Japanese and Soviet railway interests in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The filing note identifies the subject as the January 19 opening of the Manchurian freight conference. It records that the delegates reached no agreement and adjourned the discussions.

subfiles.title: Report excerpt on the Manchurian freight conference
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman
subfiles.about: Reports unsuccessful negotiations among the South Manchuria, Chinese Eastern, and Ussuri railways over restoring a freight agreement.
subfiles.summary: Soviet representatives proposed restoring the Japanese-Russian freight agreement that had lapsed during the First World War and the Russian Revolution. Representatives of the three railway systems could not agree during the two-week meeting. The issue was postponed for consideration at a future conference.

subfiles.title: Neville despatch transmitting the 1929–1930 railway annual report
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, counselor of embassy
subfiles.about: Transmits two copies of the Japanese Department of Railways annual report for the year ending March 31, 1930.
subfiles.summary: Neville sends the report from Tokyo on behalf of the ambassador. The annual report traveled under separate cover and is not reproduced here.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Neville despatch on Uchida’s resignation
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville (referenced despatch)
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to despatch no. 600 on Yasuya Uchida’s attempted resignation as president of the South Manchuria Railway.
subfiles.summary: The note links the railway file to a political report filed under 894.00 P.R./53. It identifies the dismissal of Uchida’s subordinate Eguchi as the cause of a major political controversy.

subfiles.title: Report excerpt on the attempted resignation of Yasuya Uchida
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville
subfiles.about: Describes party and military conflict over Yasuya Uchida’s attempted resignation from the South Manchuria Railway presidency.
subfiles.summary: Prime Minister Inukai struggled to select a replacement while rival Seiyukai factions promoted competing candidates. The army opposed replacing Uchida and sent a representative to Dalian to persuade him to remain through the League of Nations inquiry. Uchida agreed to stay temporarily, prompting press commentary that the military controlled the cabinet.

subfiles.title: Grew despatch transmitting the 1930–1931 railway annual report
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits two copies of the English edition of the Japanese Department of Railways annual report for the year ending March 31, 1931.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that the embassy recently received the English edition of the railway department’s annual report. The copies were transmitted under separate cover and are not included here.

subfiles.title: Grew despatch transmitting the 1931–1932 railway annual report
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits two copies of the Japanese Department of Railways annual report for the year ending March 31, 1932.
subfiles.summary: Despatch no. 488 accompanies the latest annual report of the Japanese railway administration. The report itself is not reproduced in the file text.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Grew despatch on the Shimonoseki tunnel
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew (referenced despatch)
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to despatch no. 636 concerning plans for an undersea railway tunnel between Honshu and Kyushu.
subfiles.summary: The note cross-references a political report on planning by the Japanese Railway Department. It identifies the proposed tunnel beneath the Shimonoseki straits as the report’s subject.

subfiles.title: Report excerpt on the planned Shimonoseki undersea railway
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.about: Reports progress in planning an undersea railway tunnel across the Shimonoseki straits.
subfiles.summary: Citing the Japan Times of December 17, the report states that the Railway Department’s Planning Bureau was rapidly formulating the project. The tunnel would connect Honshu with Kyushu and was expected to cost between twenty and thirty million yen.

subfiles.title: Hamilton memorandum recommending oral discouragement of locomotive credit
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck and routed State Department offices
subfiles.about: Recommends that the State Department informally discourage the proposed credit-financed locomotive sale without issuing a written reply.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum observes that no known law prohibited the Lehigh Valley Railroad transaction or similar credits to Japanese interests. Nevertheless, the government was then discouraging transactions with Japan on a credit basis. It recommends that Herbert Feis communicate this position orally to Frank C. Wright and return his enclosure without a substantive written response.

subfiles.title: Green memorandum on Wright’s initial locomotive-sale inquiry
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Records Frank C. Wright’s inquiry about government objections to a proposed Japanese purchase of 42 idle locomotives.
subfiles.summary: Wright told Green that the locomotives required about six months of repairs and were presumed destined for the South Manchuria Railroad. The proposed terms combined an advance for repairs with four annual payments of $150,000 at four percent interest. Wright emphasized the employment benefit to the Lehigh Valley Railroad and the possibility that proceeds might be applied to its government debt, while Green deferred an opinion pending consultation.

subfiles.title: Wright letter requesting State Department guidance
subfiles.from: Frank C. Wright, Reconstruction Finance Corporation
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Green, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Formally requests the State Department’s view on the Lehigh Valley Railroad’s proposed sale of 42 reconditioned locomotives to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Wright confirms his telephone conversation with Green and encloses President Kerr’s letter. He describes a $639,766 purchase price, with $39,766 due upon signing and $600,000 payable in four annual installments at four percent interest; Japanese funds would separately cover reconditioning. He asks for guidance that could be conveyed to the railroad.

subfiles.title: Kerr letter concerning the Japanese locomotive purchase
subfiles.from: Duncan J. Kerr, president of the Lehigh Valley Railroad
subfiles.about: Seeks Wright’s assistance in completing the proposed sale and repair of 42 locomotives for the Japanese government.
subfiles.summary: Kerr identifies Itaru Ninomiya as the Japanese government’s representative and explains that repairing the equipment at Sayre would provide substantial employment. After repair, the locomotives would be moved to Claremont Terminal in Jersey City and loaded onto a Japanese vessel. Kerr encloses a memorandum and detailed equipment statement.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of values and payment terms for 42 locomotives
subfiles.from: Lehigh Valley Railroad Company
subfiles.to: Prospective Japanese purchasers and reviewing officials
subfiles.about: Sets out the valuation, repair expenses, delivery conditions, and financing proposal for the locomotive sale.
subfiles.summary: The 42 locomotives had a depreciated book value of $639,766 and required $116,125.74 in repairs, producing a total operating-condition value of $755,891.74. Ninomiya proposed paying the repair cost and $39,766 of book value upon signing, with the remaining $600,000 paid in four annual installments through 1942 at four percent interest. Delivery would be f.o.b. Claremont Terminal, and the eventual contract might be made with Heavy Industries Corporation, the South Manchuria Railway, or an American corporation selected on Daniel O. Hastings’s advice.

subfiles.title: Detailed schedule of available Lehigh Valley locomotives
subfiles.from: Lehigh Valley Railroad Company
subfiles.to: Prospective Japanese purchasers and reviewing officials
subfiles.about: Lists the identifying numbers, classes, construction dates, book values, repair costs, and operating values of the 42 locomotives offered for sale.
subfiles.summary: The schedule itemizes locomotive classes N-6, N-2, N-2½, N-3, N-4, J-25, J-56½, and K-5½, built or rebuilt between 1912 and 1923. Aggregate book value was $639,766, estimated repairs were $116,125.74, and total operating-condition value was $755,891.74. It also provides average values and repair costs per locomotive.

subfiles.title: Green memorandum recording the State Department’s oral response
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, Division of Controls
subfiles.to: Department of State record and reviewing offices
subfiles.about: Records the oral communication by which the State Department discreetly discouraged the credit-financed locomotive sale.
subfiles.summary: After Wright requested an immediate answer, Green consulted Hornbeck, Feis, and Hamilton and declined to reply formally to Wright’s letter. Green suggested that Wright tell the railroad he inferred the Department would prefer it not to enter the proposed credit transaction. Wright agreed to express disapproval in his own name and to avoid directly attributing a position to the Department.

interest: The file is valuable because it links physical railway modernization with corruption, party politics, military influence, and international economic policy across the 1930s. The 1939 papers are unusually detailed: they preserve a complete commercial proposal, repair and labor estimates, financing arrangements, shipment plans, and an itemized roster of 42 locomotives. They also reveal how the State Department sought to discourage credit to Japanese interests through carefully deniable oral guidance rather than a legal ban or written ruling.
